news.title: The Marghi: Damboa’s first people
news.body:
The first people of Damboa are the Marghi. Their own traditions say they came down from the Mandara mountains and the highlands of what is now northern Cameroon, moving not all at once but clan by clan – a clan is called a fal in Marghi. As the Borno kingdom grew stronger, many Marghi groups drifted further south, and by about the fourteenth century they were living on the open plains they still farm today.

Scholars describe several branches of the Marghi. The "Plain Marghi", or Marghi babal, live in the Gwoza and Damboa districts. The Marghi Putai, in the west around Damboa and Chibok, lived closest to the Kanuri and took on much of their culture; their chiefs were called Mai. Among other Marghi groups the chief is the Ptil, advised by a council of elders.

The Marghi are, above all, farmers. Being known as a great farmer has always been a man’s pride. Before colonial times families lived in round and rectangular mud houses with thatched roofs, fenced with dried corn stalks. Over the centuries the Marghi also learned to live alongside their neighbours – Kanuri, Kilba and Babur – and most Marghi people speak two or three languages.

Do you know the story of how your family or village came to Damboa? Share it with the archive below.

sources.name: Neptune Prime – Brief history of Marghi, by Sunday Ijuptil Buba

news.title: How the calabash made Damboa a meeting place
news.body:
Long before roads and lorries, Damboa was known for one crop above others: the calabash. Grown on the farms around the town, dried and cleaned, the calabash became bowls, water carriers, ladles and food covers in homes across Borno. In northeastern Nigeria calabashes are also an art form, their golden-brown shells etched with fine patterns of animals, people and shapes.

The calabash trade brought money to Damboa, and money brought traders. Kanuri merchants began travelling back and forth to buy calabash. Many of them stayed, built homes and married into Marghi families. Over the generations this created the Damboa we know: many families are part Marghi and part Kanuri, while some remain fully Marghi or fully Kanuri.

Today Damboa is still sometimes called "Marghi State", and its motto, "Centre of Agriculture and Commerce", goes back to these days of farming and trade. The mixed heritage is one of the town’s strengths – a place where different peoples have long met, traded and become one community.

sources.name: Penn Museum – Calabashes in Northern Nigeria

news.title: Smiths and hunters of Damboa
news.body:
Damboa’s farms and market were not its only fame. The town was also known for skilled smiths. Reporters writing about Damboa in 2014 noted that the town had a guild of craftsmen who made long guns for local hunters.

These were the "Dane guns" found across West Africa. The name goes back to long-barrelled flintlock muskets that Danish and Norwegian traders brought to the coast before the mid-1800s. Over time local blacksmiths learned to make their own, and the guns replaced the bow and spear for hunting game. In a district on the edge of the Sambisa bush, hunting was part of everyday life, and hunters’ groups were respected members of the community.

The smiths’ fire, hammer and anvil also made hoes, axes and knives for farmers – the tools that fed Damboa. We would like to record this craft before it is forgotten. If your family were smiths or hunters, please tell us their story.
news.source_name: Council on Foreign Relations (citing the Wall Street Journal)

news.title: Sambisa: when Damboa’s forest drew safari visitors
news.body:
Part of the great Sambisa Forest lies within Damboa. Its name comes from Sambisa village, on the border with Gwoza. The forest covers about 518 square kilometres, and in colonial times a Sambisa Game Reserve covered more than 2,200 square kilometres in its eastern part.

From around 1970 the reserve became a safari destination. Visitors stayed in cabins and lodges to watch leopards, lions, elephants and hyenas. Bird experts recorded 62 species there, and Sambisa was once thought to be the last place in Nigeria where wild ostriches lived. In 1991 the Borno State Government made the reserve part of the Chad Basin National Park.

The forest suffered badly from poaching, tree-cutting and, from 2013, insurgency: the lodges fell down, roads became overgrown and the animals declined. But the memory of Sambisa as a place of wildlife and visitors is part of Damboa’s heritage – and a hope for the future.

news.title: Borno State and Damboa Local Government are born
news.body:
On 3 February 1976 the military Head of State, General Murtala Mohammed, created seven new states, Borno among them, out of the old North-Eastern State. It was one of the most important days in Nigeria’s administrative history – and it came just ten days before he was killed in a failed coup. Group Captain Mustapha Amin became the first Governor of Borno State in March 1976.

The same year the national Local Government Reform set up local government councils as a third tier of government, and Damboa Local Government Area was created, with its headquarters in Damboa town. The reform gave elected councils responsibility for local services, while traditional rulers kept their role as custodians of culture and tradition.

The full list of Damboa’s chairmen since 1976 is being compiled from council records. If you have photos or documents from the council’s early years, please share them.
news.source_name: Daily Trust – X-raying Murtala’s 7 states at 50

sources.name: Wikipedia – List of governors of Borno State

news.title: The hard year: Damboa under attack
news.body:
2014 was the hardest year in Damboa’s modern history. In January insurgents attacked the army base in the town and were driven back. On 4 July they returned with a larger force and attacked the base and the police station, and many families fled.

On 18 July 2014 the town itself was overrun. Homes were set on fire and many people were killed; eyewitnesses said half of Damboa was burnt, including the main market. Telephone lines were cut, and the National Emergency Management Agency reported that more than 15,000 people were driven from their homes, most of them to Maiduguri.

Damboa remembers everyone who lost their lives that year, and honours the soldiers, police, hunters and young volunteers who stood to defend the town. Families who wish to have a loved one remembered in this archive may contact the Information Unit.

news.title: Troops retake Damboa
news.body:
Weeks after the town fell, Nigerian troops pushed back into Damboa. By late August 2014 the insurgents had been driven out, and the flag they had raised over the town was pulled down.

The fight was not over. In the months that followed attackers tried several times to re-enter the town and were repelled by the army’s 195 Battalion. Damboa became a garrison town, and the Maiduguri road was often dangerous.

But retaking the town was the first step on the long road home. For the thousands of Damboa families living in camps and with relatives in Maiduguri, it meant that one day they could return.
news.source_name: ICIR Nigeria – Nigerian Military Reclaims Damboa

news.title: The road home
news.body:
Return began with the road. As the military reopened the Maiduguri–Damboa–Biu highway, vehicles started to run again, at first under escort. The Damboa motor park filled with buses and lorries, carrying traders, farmers and families back to the town.

People came home to burnt houses and empty streets, and began again. Families repaired their compounds, farmers went back to the land closest to town, and traders set up wherever they could. Aid agencies brought food, water and health care to returnees and to those still displaced.

Each family that returned made it easier for the next. Slowly, Damboa came back to life.
news.source_name: ICIR Nigeria – Life after Boko Haram: residents return home

news.title: Damboa market reopens after two years
news.body:
On Tuesday 6 September 2016 the Damboa township market opened its gates again, two years after it was closed by the attacks of 2014. The caretaker chairman of the council, Alhaji Abu Hong, performed the reopening at a ceremony in Damboa, saying the market could reopen because peace had returned to the area.

He urged traders to be security-conscious and to work with the security agencies to keep the peace. The District Head of Damboa, Malam Abdullahi Damboa, said he was happy to see the market open again and pledged his support to the state government in keeping the market peaceful.

For a town built on trade, the reopening of the market was a turning point: it brought buyers from the villages, gave work to traders and porters, and showed everyone that Damboa was open for business again.
news.source_name: Tribune Online – Damboa LG re-opens Damboa market as peace returns to Borno

sources.name: Vanguard – Damboa market, shut after 2014 attacks, re-opens
ICIR Nigeria – Popular market near Sambisa re-opens

news.title: The Monday livestock market returns
news.body:
On Monday 25 March 2024 the famous Damboa Monday Market – the livestock market – reopened, and buyers and sellers came from across Borno State and beyond.

Residents described it as a wonderful day and a clear sign that relative peace, security and stability had returned. Livestock dealers came in from the surrounding villages with cattle, sheep and goats, and townspeople expected the market to bring visitors and business back to Damboa.

The return of the Monday Market completed the story that began with the township market in 2016: Damboa was once again a centre of agriculture and commerce for southern Borno.
news.source_name: Radio Ndarason Internationale – Excitement as popular Damboa livestock market reopens

settings.welcome_en: In line with the transformation agenda of His Excellency, Prof. Babagana Umara Zulum, mni, FNSE, Executive Governor of Borno State, I welcome you to the official website of Damboa Local Government. Dear people of Damboa, this website is our new front door. Here you will find what your council is doing, the projects in every ward, and how to reach us. It belongs to all of us, across every ward and every community. Tell us what you need, follow our progress, and hold us to our promises. Together we will keep building a Damboa we are proud of.
settings.welcome_ha: Bisa tsarin sauyi na Mai Girma Gwamna, Farfesa Babagana Umara Zulum, mni, FNSE, Gwamnan Jihar Borno, ina maraba da ku zuwa shafin hukuma na Karamar Hukumar Damboa. Ya ku al'ummar Damboa, wannan shafin shi ne sabuwar kofarmu. A nan za ku ga abin da karamar hukumarku ke yi, ayyukan da ake yi a kowace mazaba, da yadda za ku same mu. Namu ne baki daya, a kowace mazaba da kowace al'umma. Ku fada mana bukatunku, ku bi ci gabanmu, ku kuma rike mu da alkawuranmu. Tare za mu ci gaba da gina Damboa da za mu yi alfahari da ita.
settings.hero_en: The home of the Marghi people and a centre of agriculture and commerce in southern Borno. Rebuilding, reconnecting and moving forward together.
settings.hero_ha: Gidan al'ummar Marghi kuma cibiyar noma da kasuwanci a kudancin Borno. Muna sake ginawa, sake hadewa da ci gaba tare.
